item.title: Show, don’t tell: Sophos AI at CAMLIS
item.description:
For the fourth year running, Sophos AI will share new research at the Conference on Applied Machine Learning in Information Security (CAMLIS). On October 23, Senior AI/ML Engineer Tamás Nyiri will lead a poster session entitled “Show, Don’t Tell: Calibrating Agentic SOC Analysts via Hierarchical Evidence Graphs.”

This research turns traces used in agentic investigations into features for a traditional ML model, which helps calibrate the agent’s verdicts and flag the cases it most likely got wrong.

A matter of fact

SOCs increasingly use AI agents to investigate alerts. Those agents extract entities and context connected to alerts, plan investigation steps, query tools, and produce reports containing final verdict.

While such agents can save analysts time, they can also fail in both predictable and surprising ways. An agent may treat a failed or missing check as evidence that nothing is wrong, link events simply because they happened close together, judge a legitimate installer or developer tool by its behavior alone, or close a case prematurely. These mistakes can be hard to spot, especially since reports tend to tell a confident story, while the evidence is buried in a long investigation trace.

Motivated by this challenge, Tamás developed an approach that makes an investigation agent show its evidence. First, the investigation steps are converted into a ‘fact graph,’ with the agent’s report and verdict withheld. Structured trace fields are parsed, while an LLM extracts meaning from free text under a fixed schema. The graph records what was observed, which tool calls failed, and how entities relate to one another. It also infers what is missing, such as unexamined alternative explanations and unqueried sources.

The fact graph is useful on its own, but here it serves as a building block for three evidence views:

  • Coverage: were the necessary checks actually run?
  • Context: do events link to the right entity, and is there a benign explanation?
  • Readiness: does the evidence justify a decision?

Features from these views feed a simple supervised model that estimates how likely a senior reviewer is to disagree with the agent’s verdict.

Show me the results

The training labels come from a two-stage human review. First, an analyst examines each agent investigation and gives a verdict; a senior analyst then reviews both and sets the final verdict, which serves as ground truth. The model is a regularized logistic regression, fit separately for three yes/no questions:

  1. Is the investigation conclusive?
  2. Is the initial alert a true positive
  3. Is the underlying content malicious in nature?

Alongside the evidence features, the model uses the agent’s verdict as a prior, based on how often reviewers agreed with that verdict in the training cases. This is necessary because labeling is costly and, at this training size, overfitting is unavoidable. Each of the 314 cases is scored by a model trained on the other 313 (leave-one-out cross-validation), so no case contributes to its own score.

The research is still at the proof-of-concept stage, with many improvements planned, but even this simple version shows an encouraging signal. Ranking cases by the model’s disagreement score brought agent errors to the front of the review queue. The senior reviewer overturned the agent’s verdict in 25% of all cases, but in 65% of the 20 highest-scoring cases: roughly 2.6 times the base rate.

During the session, Tamás will walk through the methodology, an example fact graph from a real case, and the lessons learned along the way.

If you’re attending CAMLIS, feel free to stop by Tamás’ poster to discuss your thoughts on this emerging research direction – and keep an eye out for more details of this approach in the near future.

item.title: Sophos ITDR expands identity protection for the AI era
item.description:
Identity has become one of the most targeted attack surfaces in cybersecurity, with attackers increasingly relying on stolen credentials, compromised sessions, excessive privileges, and identity misconfigurations to gain access. At the same time, organizations are managing more cloud services, remote users, non-human identities, and a rapidly growing number of AI agents that can access systems and data.

According to the Sophos State of Identity Security Report 2026, 71% of organizations experienced an identity-related breach in the past year, with weak non-human identity management linked to 41% of these breaches.

The challenge is clear: it’s not just about managing identities, it’s understanding which identities introduce risk, how those risks evolve over time, and how to respond before attackers can take advantage.

Identity security is evolving. So is Sophos ITDR.

Sophos Identity Threat Detection and Response (ITDR) was introduced in 2025 as a powerful identity security add-on for Sophos XDR and Sophos MDR. Today, as organizations navigate this expanding identity attack surface, Sophos ITDR has evolved into a standalone solution and one of the fastest ways to experience Sophos Fusion, the Sophos AI-Native Cybersecurity Defense System.

What’s new in Sophos ITDR:

Now available
standalone

Fast deployment, immediate visibility, no additional Sophos solutions required

Expanded Microsoft
support

Secures Microsoft Entra ID and on-premises Active Directory environments

Dynamic AI
identity risk scores

Continuously evaluate and explain risky identities using behavioral and environmental signals

AI identity
visibility

Discovers Microsoft AI agents, ownership relationships, permissions, and risks

160+ continuous
posture checks

Surface security gaps, excessive privileges, and identity attack paths

Contextualized cases
and direct response

Automatically group findings into cases and take key actions from one interface

Together, these enhancements help organizations move beyond identity management. Sophos ITDR supports full identity security, from visibility and prioritization to investigation and response.

Secure identity from risk to response

With a complete view of human and non-human identities and more than 160 continuous posture assessments, organizations can clearly see their users, devices, applications, groups, service accounts, and Microsoft AI agent access, owners, and permissions, at a glance.

Sophos ITDR then prioritizes what matters most through new dynamic, AI-driven identity risk scores that continuously evaluate and explain the risk of every human and non-human identity using behavioral analytics, authentication history, geolocation data, and other signals. Security teams can quickly understand who presents the greatest risk and why.

When credentials are exposed, Sophos ITDR continuously monitors dark web and breach intelligence sources and finds affected identities (with advanced monitoring of VIP accounts) and enables immediate action. High-risk findings are automatically grouped into contextualized cases that bring together identities, detections, and other risk factors all in one place. From there, organizations can respond directly from within Sophos ITDR by forcing password resets, revoking active sessions, enforcing MFA, and disabling accounts before attackers can turn exposed identities into active compromises. 

Real results in minutes

With a 30-day free trial and seamless deployment, organizations typically begin uncovering meaningful identity risks within minutes. In recent Sophos ITDR trials, organizations identified hundreds of orphaned Azure accounts, credential exposures, and critical MFA gaps that had previously gone unnoticed.

As part of Sophos Fusion, identity intelligence becomes part of a broader cyber defense strategy that connects detection, investigation, and response across endpoints, networks, cloud environments, email, and identity systems. Learn more at www.sophos.com/fusion.

item.title: ConnectWise Cloud Backup application abused in cross-tenant token sweep
item.description:
On October 15, 2026, Sophos X-Ops researchers identified a series of service principal sign-ins in which a threat actor authenticated as the ConnectWise Cloud Backup application (formerly SkyKick) and requested app-only Microsoft Graph tokens from customer Microsoft 365 tenants. The malicious scanning activity originated from a single virtual private server (VPS) and continued for about 96 minutes. X-Ops researchers found no evidence of hands-on-keyboard activity and assess with high confidence that the threat actor ran a script that enumerated a list of tenants that had consented to the application.

The sign-ins required no user password and no multi-factor authentication (MFA) because the threat actor authenticated with the application's own identity. This activity is consistent with abuse of a compromised vendor-held application credential. It is unclear how the credential was obtained or what the threat actor did with the obtained tokens.

ConnectWise published an advisory about the service interruption, as well as a technical investigation and remediation guide. The advisory notes that ConnectWise shut off Cloud Backup application access for partners and customers as a protective measure.;

Background

ConnectWise Cloud Backup is a Microsoft 365 product that operates through a multi-tenant Entra application. When a customer enables the product, they consent to the application in their tenant. This consent allows the vendor's application identity to request Microsoft Graph tokens for the tenant to read data for backup. A threat actor who obtains the application's credential can request the same tokens in every tenant that has granted consent.

Observed activity

X-Ops researchers observed the threat actor request one app-only Graph token for the Cloud Backup application in each targeted tenant. The reconnaissance began at 07:11 UTC on October 15, and the last observed scan was at 08:47 UTC. All requests originated from 144[.]172[.]64[.]128 and used the following User-Agents: Python-urllib/3.12 and python-requests/2.31.

Analysis revealed three characteristics that point to automated activity:

  • Tenants were accessed in strictly ascending tenant GUID order.
  • Requests were spaced one to six minutes apart.
  • The sweep included tenants with no active backup subscription, which suggests the threat actor worked from a full list of tenants that had consented to the application, including those that were no longer active backup customers.

As of this publication, there is no evidence that the application created new secrets, applications, consents, or role assignments in the reviewed tenants.

Recommendations

Organizations that use or have ever used ConnectWise Cloud Backup or SkyKick products should take the following actions:

  • Review Entra enterprise applications and remove consent for the applications that ConnectWise disabled.
  • Review Entra sign-in logs during the October 15-17 timeframe, specifically service principal sign-ins for the indicators that have been associated with this activity.
  • Review audit logs for new credentials, secrets, application registrations, consents, and role assignments made by these applications since October 13.
  • Retrieve Microsoft Graph activity logs for tenants with active backup, if available, to evaluate how issued tokens were used.
  • Follow the vendor's remediation guidance, including credential rotation steps.

Countermeasures and indicators

SophosLabs continues to monitor the threat landscape for activity related to this incident and will deliver detections and protections as available.

The indicators in Table 1 can be used to detect activity related to this threat. Note that IP addresses can be reallocated.

item.title: Beyond the mailbox: Graph reconnaissance and ServiceNow user enumeration in a modern identity intrusion
item.description:
Traditional business email compromise (BEC) is often thought of as a mailbox problem: a stolen account, unauthorized access to email, forwarding rules, and (sometimes) outgoing mail impersonating the compromised user. But more recent incidents show how far beyond “email only” these intrusions can extend once an attacker gains control of a cloud identity.

In a recent case investigated by the Sophos X-Ops Incident Response team, a threat actor used voice phishing (vishing) and self-service password reset (SSPR) abuse to take over a Microsoft 365 account, establish a Primary Refresh Token (PRT)-backed device session, and pivot into multiple SaaS platforms. Rather than stopping at mailbox access, the actor treated the compromised identity as a springboard into the target’s broader SaaS estate.

Post-compromise activity was identified from a single compromised user account and included Microsoft Graph reconnaissance, access to email and SharePoint content including the download of nearly 100,000 documents, access to Salesforce, and a confirmed user-table export from ServiceNow of approximately 2,500 records. 

The Sophos X-Ops Incident Response team works with customers who have not previously purchased other Sophos offerings such as XDR. At the end of this writeup, we briefly cover the proactive, reactive, and behavioral protections available from Sophos via our other service offerings.

Initial access: SSPR abuse enabled by vishing

The compromise began with self-service password reset (SSPR) abuse. After several employees reported receiving suspicious phone calls from a suspected threat actor, the targeted organization sent a company-wide email warning users of the attack. However, one user had already unknowingly been compromised prior to the issuance of the emailed warning. The affected user later reported that the threat actor called by phone, impersonated help desk personnel, and convinced the user to provide the SMS-based MFA verification code needed to complete the reset flow.

Telemetry shows that an earlier SSPR initiation occurred from a geographically anomalous IP address the day before the confirmed vishing event. It is not clear whether that earlier attempt was directly related, but it may represent precursor probing or an unsuccessful attempt to validate the account. The confirmed compromise occurred when the actor initiated another SSPR flow from a different attacker-controlled IP, completed SMS verification, and successfully reset the user’s password.

This initial access method is important because it bypassed the need for a phishing page, malware, or an OAuth consent prompt. The user’s participation in a legitimate account recovery workflow was enough to hand over control of the identity.

From password reset to token-backed session

Within minutes of the successful password reset, the actor went beyond simple sign-in activity and established a device-backed cloud session.

The sequence included:

  • Entra ID registration of a new Windows device
  • successful use of a Primary Refresh Token
  • subsequent Microsoft Edge authentication using that token-backed device context

The actor established a persistent authenticated session tied to a newly registered Entra ID device, which gave them a more durable foothold than a single password-based web login.

In the sign-in records reviewed during the investigation, later access to ServiceNow was recorded as SAML 2.0 authentication using a primary refresh token, with MFA listed as “Previously satisfied.” That combination strongly suggests the actor was leveraging an already-authenticated Microsoft cloud session to access federated downstream applications, rather than performing repeated fully interactive reauthentication for each platform.

Immediate post-compromise activity in Microsoft 365

After gaining access to the account, the actor signed in to My Apps, Microsoft Graph, and Salesforce. Logs indicate the threat actor accessed emails, downloaded SharePoint documents, and launched Microsoft Teams. Microsoft Graph was used for initial reconnaissance, and over the course of the next day the actor began to sign in to additional applications, including ServiceNow.

This is not extraordinary behavior for a modern attacker. Once a threat actor has a valid session in the identity provider, they can enumerate accessible resources and pivot into downstream services. Mandiant’s reporting on recent GOLD CRYSTAL (ShinyHunters) linked and adjacent SaaS extortion activity has described this exact operational shift, where vishing and credential harvesting are used to obtain SSO access and then fan out into cloud applications for reconnaissance and data theft.

Structured Graph API reconnaissance

Sophos’s analysis of logs from GraphApiAuditEvents from Microsoft Defender identified evidence the threat actor’s activity included Graph API-driven reconnaissance queries consistent with:

  • Validating user context and licensing
  • Retrieving organization metadata
  • Enumerating tenant relationships
  • Mapping directory roles and effective permissions
  • Enumerating enterprise applications and service principals
  • Identifying verified tenant domains
  • Enumerating individual users and larger sets of directory objects

Examples of the query patterns documented during analysis included the following:

  • hxxps[://]graph[.]microsoft[.]com/v1[.]0/me/licenseDetails
  • hxxps[://]graph[.]microsoft[.]com/v1[.]0/organization
  • hxxps[://]graph[.]microsoft[.]com/beta/tenantRelationships/getResourceTenants?$select=tenantId
  • hxxps[://]graph[.]microsoft[.]com/beta/users/{id}/roleManagement/directory/transitiveRoleAssignments?$count=true
  • hxxps[://]graph[.]microsoft[.]com/beta/users/{id}/ownedObjects/Microsoft[.]graph[.]ServicePrincipal?$top=999
  • hxxps[://]graph[.]microsoft[.]com/v1[.]0/domains
  • hxxps[://]graph[.]microsoft[.]com/v1[.]0/sites
  • hxxps[://]graph[.]microsoft[.]com/v1[.]0/users/{UPN}?$select=userPrincipalName
  • hxxps[://]graph[.]microsoft[.]com/v1[.]0/users/$count 

Impact

The primary impact of the incident involved access to email and SharePoint data.

Sophos’s analysis of Microsoft’s Unified Audit Logs identified:

  • Over 100 unique mail items accessed across the compromised user’s mailbox and multiple shared mailboxes to which they had access
  • Approximately 100,000 unique SharePoint files downloaded

Access to emails is commonly the primary focus of BEC incidents, but this case shows how valuable a target SharePoint can be.

The threat actor accessed a relatively small number of mail items compared to the SharePoint files downloaded. A review of the subject lines of the emails accessed by the threat actor revealed a search pattern for messages related to account or credential related messages, customer information, internal organizational/team structure, and workflow approval-style emails. One of the messages reviewed by the actor was the organization's own vishing-awareness notification; that same message was subsequently deleted from the mailbox, demonstrating that the actor read and confirmed the organization was aware of the campaign before suppressing it from the compromised user's view.

For SharePoint, logs for SearchQueryInitiatedSharePoint indicate the threat actor searched for key terms with an apparent intent of identifying credentials, Personally Identifiable Information (PII), and information about product development and customers. Notably, four of the recovered queries, including several misspelled variants, targeted the organization's identity verification vendor by name, suggesting the actor either had prior knowledge of which MFA platform was in use or was specifically searching for documentation that might support a bypass.

A sample of keywords searched by the threat actor in this attack includes:

  • Salesforce
  • IT
  • Sales
  • Aws
  • NDA
  • Contracts
  • Login
  • Cred
  • Engineering
  • Customers
  • Jira
  • SSN
  • Contacts
  • Password
  • VPN
  • SSH 

Downstream SaaS pivot #1: Salesforce

The actor also pivoted into Salesforce using federated sign-in.

Entra sign-in telemetry showed multiple successful SAML-based accesses to Salesforce shortly after the attacker established the Microsoft cloud session. The reviewed Salesforce logs support the conclusion that the actor successfully accessed Salesforce, but the evidence reviewed in this case did not show large-scale CRM data extraction.

Salesforce logs showed a “SuspiciousActivity” event followed by successful execution of “FreezeUser” and “SendEmail”, indicating that Salesforce's automated anomaly-detection containment triggered, freezing the account and notifying the customer's Salesforce administrator.

Downstream SaaS pivot #2: ServiceNow

The largest non-Microsoft impact in this case came from attacker access to ServiceNow.

Entra telemetry showed a successful federated sign-in to the organization’s ServiceNow tenant. Subsequent ServiceNow logs from the same user context showed:

  • A successful login and session establishment
  • Navigation through dashboard views
  • Repeated access to the sys_user list view
  • Export activity targeting sys_user
  • Read access to the generated attachment sys_user.csv

Related export metadata indicated that the resulting CSV contained approximately 2,500 records.

The sys_user table that was targeted stores a record of everyone who logs in or interacts with ServiceNow and can include details such as name, email, phone number, roles, department, and manager. The presence of specific fields depends on the organization’s configuration settings. 

The information gathered from this would give the threat actor insight into:

  • Who exists in the platform
  • How user accounts are structured
  • How the organization is modeled

Combined with the contact information listed there, this information could be sold or used to conduct additional, more convincing social engineering attacks. In this case, the organization continued to receive numerous phishing and vishing attempts which may have utilized such information.

Notably, the same session later touched the CMDB [Configuration Management Database] Computer (cmdb_ci_computer) list view, indicating at least some additional browsing beyond the user directory. This can contain information about hardware inventory including computer names and operating systems. However, no evidence of export from that table was identified. 

Microsoft Teams access

Purview logs contained a TeamsSessionStarted operation performed by the threat actor, indicating Microsoft Teams was launched. Microsoft records events for activities such as message creation, edits, deletions, participant additions, and the creation of new chats or teams, but it does not audit the passive viewing of existing messages in chats and channels a user already has access to. This is a commonly overlooked gap. Threat actors can gather significant sensitive information through passive reconnaissance of Teams chats without leaving any audit trail of what was read.

Defense evasion and cleanup

The actor did not create inbox rules, forwarding rules, or new applications — a notable absence in a case that otherwise resembles modern BEC and SaaS intrusion playbooks.

Instead, the only observed cleanup behavior in Exchange was the deletion of two messages:

  • One warning users about active vishing attempts in the environment
  • One additional message of unknown content

That first deletion is particularly telling. The organization had already begun warning users about the scam calls, but the compromised user was kept from seeing that warning because the actor removed it from their mailbox.

Recommendations

This intrusion is a useful illustration that identity-centric attacks no longer stop at the mailbox. The recommendations below are scoped to the specific behaviors observed in this case and are prioritized by the leverage they would have given defenders against this exact intrusion path.

Harden the account recovery surface, not just sign-in

The compromise began with self-service password reset (SSPR) abuse. The affected user later reported that the threat actor called by phone, impersonated help desk personnel, and convinced the user to provide the SMS-based MFA verification code needed to complete the reset flow.

item.title: Why Incident Response Demand Will Grow Faster than Expected
item.description:
This article is part of an ongoing series from Sophos frontline security operations specialists, sharing the expertise they use to strengthen our industry-leading Managed Detection and Response (MDR) service and defend customers against evolving AI-era threats.

A 20% growth forecast for cybersecurity talent sounds significant. I believe it understates what we are going to see in Incident Response. 

The U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics projects 21% employment growth for information security analysts between 2025 and 2035. That projection applies to the broader information security profession, not specifically to Incident Response. Still, it gives us a useful benchmark. 

Based on what I am seeing and hearing across the industry, Incident Response demand could grow much faster. 

I attend security conferences where leaders from other firms openly say they are hiring Incident Response analysts. Our partners tell us they are hiring. DFIR firms we know are asking whether they can use Sophos to provide overflow support when their teams reach capacity. 

These are not isolated conversations. They are consistent signals from across the security ecosystem. 

Everyone is looking for more Incident Response capacity.

AI is giving attackers greater scale 

AI has changed what threat actors can accomplish with the people and resources they already have. 

Attackers still rely on many of the same techniques. They steal credentials, exploit vulnerabilities, use social engineering, move laterally, and target critical systems. What is changing is the speed and scale at which they can do it. 

The Sophos AI Security 2026 Report found that AI is compressing attack timelines rather than creating entirely new categories of attacks. It is enabling both attackers and defenders to move faster through familiar operations. 

That distinction is important. 

We do not need to wait for a fully autonomous AI attacker before treating this as a serious capacity problem. If AI helps an attacker research more targets, create more convincing lures, analyze more code, or identify more opportunities, the attacker has already become more productive. 

The 2026 Sophos Active Adversary Report describes the effect as more speed, volume, and noise in the threat landscape, even while attackers continue to use many of the same tools and techniques. 

Attackers have found a way to scale their operations. Most defenders have not. 

Organizations cannot patch at attacker speed 

This is especially visible in vulnerability management. 

The advice to “patch faster” is correct, but it does not reflect the full operational challenge. A security team cannot simply install every update as soon as it becomes available. 

Organizations need to know which systems are affected. They need to understand business criticality, test changes, coordinate maintenance windows, manage legacy technology, and confirm that remediation has worked. In some environments, a rushed update can create a significant operational outage. 

AI is accelerating vulnerability discovery and shortening the path between disclosure and exploitation. This raises the pressure on security teams that are already managing complex environments with limited resources. 

Many organizations simply do not have enough people to patch every system as quickly as the current threat environment requires. 

That does not necessarily mean they have a bad security program. It means their available capacity has not grown at the same rate as the problem. 

The gap between attacker speed and defender capacity is getting wider.

The challenge goes beyond patching

Patching is only part of the issue. 

Analysis of 661 incidents in the 2026 Sophos Active Adversary Report found that 67% of intrusions began with compromised credentials or other identity-related tactics. Attackers reached Active Directory in an average of three hours and 24 minutes. 

That leaves very little room for delay. 

Organizations need to patch vulnerable systems, strengthen identity controls, retain the right telemetry, monitor suspicious behavior, and provide coverage outside normal business hours. They also need a tested plan for what happens when those controls fail. 

At some point, almost every organization will need help answering four basic questions: 

  • What happened?
  • How far did the attacker get?
  • What do we need to contain?
  • What do we need to do next?

Those questions require experienced Incident Response professionals. 

Technology helps, but experience still matters 

AI and automation will make Incident Response teams more productive. 

They can help responders collect evidence, correlate information, summarize activity, identify patterns, and focus their attention on the areas that matter most. We should embrace those capabilities. 

But a serious security incident is not simply a technical investigation.

item.title: BRONZE SANDCASTLE deploys modified Meterpreter shells
item.description:
Counter Threat Unit™ (CTU) and SophosLabs researchers investigated a cluster of incidents attributed to the BRONZE SANDCASTLE threat group. The most distinctive technical marker for BRONZE SANDCASTLE is its consistent use of Sandboxie DLL sideloading.

DLL sideloading details

Across multiple victims’ environments, legitimate Sandboxie executables were placed alongside a malicious sbiedll.dll file, causing the trusted application to load attacker-controlled code at runtime. This consistent pattern functions as a signature for the group, although the threat actors employ several other sideloading file combinations as well (see Table 1).

Legitimate fileMalicious sideloaded DLL
SandboxieWUAU.exe (Sandboxie)sbiedll.dll
Start.exe (renamed Sandboxie executable)sbiedll.dll
javaw.exe (Java application)jli.dll
Krita.exe (Krita digital painting)Krita.dll
NvdaHelper.exe (NVDA NonVisual Desktop Access)NvdaHelperRemote.dll
Jcef_helper.exe (Java Chromium Embedded Framework Helper)Libcef.dll
Vmmap.exe (Sysinternals process memory analyzer)Version.dll
LineAppMgr.exe (LINE messaging application)msvcp140.dll
bginfo64.exe (Sysinternals utility that displays system information)snmpapi.dll

Table 1: DLL sideloading files used by BRONZE SANDCASTLE

The sideloaded DLLs typically read and execute payloads stored in encrypted config.ini files. This design minimizes static detection and allows operators to adjust behavior without replacing DLL binaries. Renamed legitimate executables are frequently used to blend into victims’ environments, with execution resulting in in-memory shellcode activity rather than additional disk artifacts. Figure 1 shows the components of a sample ZIP archive (aez.zip) on a compromised system: the clean loader (javaw.exe), the sideloaded DLL (jli.dll), and the file containing the encrypted payload (config.ini).

Figure 1: Sample DLL sideloading components deployed in a ZIP archive on a compromised system

The malicious DLL code implements a flattened control-flow dispatcher that obscures program logic by using a virtualized state machine instead of direct branches (see Figure 2).

Figure 2: Core sequence of the DLL’s code obfuscation

A state value indexes a per-state table, and a value from the table is passed through a custom bit-mixing routine using byte swapping, variable rotations, inversion, and negation. The result is used as an index into a jump table of code pointers, and execution continues via an indirect jump. Some indices intentionally resolve to fall-through locations, further complicating static analysis and obscuring the program’s true control flow.

Payload

The decrypted payload is a backdoor program. Once loaded and decoded by the DLL, config.ini superficially resembles a Windows executable in memory (see Figure 3).

Figure 3: Decoded config.ini file in memory

The file header is a position‑independent PE loader and execution stub, often referred to as a reflective loader. The payload exhibits structural similarities to stageless shellcode payloads such as those generated by the Metasploit Framework (MSF), including position-independent execution, manual PE validation, and in-memory loading of an embedded executable. However, several implementation details indicate that this loader is not a standard Metasploit artifact. In particular, the API resolution logic uses non-standard hashing and transformation routines rather than the well-known ROR13 algorithm used by Metasploit, and the codebase is significantly larger and more complex than typical MSF shellcode.

The analyzed samples also contain elements of the well-known COFFLoader project (see Figure 4). The use of standard APIs from this project suggests that the malware author employed a custom Beacon Object File (BOF) to create their own post-exploitation features.

Figure 4: COFFLoader elements observed in compromised systems’ memory

Additional in-memory strings associated with C++ function decorators demonstrate the data-stealing capabilities that BRONZE SANDCASTLE builds into its payload (see Figure 5).

Figure 5: In-memory strings from BRONZE SANDCASTLE's payload

Sophos analysts identified two versions of the payload: 1.1.5 and 1.1.7. Once running, the payload sends a structured JSON object with nested “info” block to its command and control (C2) server (see Figure 6). The following information is included in that block:

  • Host identifiers: hostname, username, GUID, domain
  • OS version (e.g.,10.0.19042)
  • Internal IP address
  • Public IP address
  • Process listing and metadata (PID, process name, execution method)
  • Working directory
  • Code page
  • CPU architecture
  • Implant start time
  • Implant type (server/client)

Figure 6: Formatted JSON info block in version 1.1.7

CTU™ researchers observed instances of the payload reaching out to legitimate websites such as file[.]io, gofile[.]io, ably[.]net, and ably[.]io, possibly to receive C2 tasking from the operators. Version 1.1.5 contacted C2 servers dc[.]cathaypacifice[.]com and net[.]dpworldto[.]com. Version 1.1.7 payloads have also been observed communicating with github[.]com repositories to download encrypted config files (see Figure 7).

Figure 7: Payload attempting to download a config file from GitHub

The GitHub repository (hxxps://api[.]github[.]com/repos/LatonyCharnleyaW) has little history, with only a few submissions (see Figure 8).

Figure 8: Overview page of LatonyCharnleyaW GitHub repo

The repository contained multiple files. Analysis suggested that the following files were likely encrypted config files: main.3ku8inqb.js.map, main.lhxjkkai.js.map, main.y8hnze7q.js.map, and README.md. There were also encrypted files with a .ts extension (see Figure 9) that may be implants used by the backdoor.

Figure 9: List of .ts files in the GitHub repository

After a payload is installed in a target environment, the threat actors use it to conduct common survey tasks such as executing Windows “net” commands to enumerate the local network and user accounts. The threat actors have also created Volume Shadow copies via vssadmin.exe prior to copying the Windows ntds.dit file. This Windows file is the central database file of Active Directory that contains user credentials, group policies, security settings, and domain configurations.

Victimology and links to China

CTU researchers have observed BRONZE SANDCASTLE targeting organizations in Asia and Africa, which is typical of several China-based threat groups, including BRONZE PRESIDENT and BRONZE ATLAS. Although the geographic targeting overlaps with that of these groups, the observed activity could not be reliably linked to either group and exhibited distinctive technical characteristics. CTU researchers consequently created the separate BRONZE SANDCASTLE designation to represent the group behind this activity.

CTU analysis of incidents between August 2025 and August 2026 revealed victims in the Philippines, Taiwan, Afghanistan, Namibia, and likely also the Republic of Korea (see Figure 10).

Figure 10: Distribution of BRONZE SANDCASTLE victims in incidents between August 2025 and August 2026

Observations that the threat actors are most active in UTC+8 time (see Figure 11) reinforces attribution to a China-based threat group. The active hours align with the 996 working hour system that is particularly popular in China’s tech sector.

Figure 11: Heatmap of BRONZE SANDCASTLE activity by hour of the day

The details of the observed loaders and the novel Meterpreter-based payload appear to be specific to BRONZE SANDCASTLE.

Recommendations

Organizations at risk of targeting by China’s intelligence-gathering operations should familiarize themselves with BRONZE SANDCASTLE’s tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs). The threat group predominantly uses encrypted payload and configuration files that are decoded at runtime, meaning that static file-based detections may be ineffective. Organizations should instead focus on behavioral indicators such as DLLs reading local files followed by immediate in-memory execution, which may indicate decoding and staging activity. Endpoint telemetry and memory-based detection are essential. Security teams should enable monitoring for reflective loading patterns, anomalous PE headers in memory, and processes exhibiting characteristics of position-independent shellcode execution.

Countermeasures and indicators

The following Sophos countermeasures relate to this threat:

  • ATK/Swrort-Y
  • ATK/ScLoad-W
  • ATK/ScLoad-X
  • ATK/ScLoad-Y
  • ATK/ScLoad-Z
  • Troj/Loader-JL
  • Troj/Loader-JP

Due to the large number of threat indicators, the full list is available in the SophosLabs GitHub repository.

Acknowledgements

Thanks to Colin Cowie, Jordon Olness, and Morgan Demboski for their analysis and insight into this activity.

item.title: Web App Owners – You’re on Notice. Your Low-Hanging Fruit Just Got Lower
item.description:
This article is part of an ongoing series from Sophos frontline security operations specialists, sharing the expertise they use to strengthen our industry-leading Managed Detection and Response (MDR) service and defend customers against evolving AI-era threats.

The cybersecurity industry has spent years preparing for attackers who automate reconnaissance, vulnerability scanning, and credential attacks. What is changing now is the degree to which automation can connect those individual activities into a sustained intrusion workflow.

Recent Sophos Incident Response investigations illustrate this shift. The incidents affected unrelated organizations in different industries and relied on different initial-access paths. Yet the operational patterns were strikingly similar: rapid reconnaissance, repetitive testing, credential discovery, privilege-escalation attempts, lateral movement, data-access validation, persistence, and systematic cleanup.

The evidence points to the use of systems consistent with machine-speed tooling likely associated with the use of an AI agent or orchestration framework. There were no user-agent strings, or specific signatures that called out AI-based tools.  However, the speed, breadth, repetition, and adaptability observed in the incidents demonstrate why distinguishing between a skilled operator, scripted automation, and an AI-assisted attacker is becoming increasingly difficult.

More importantly, defenders may soon find that the distinction matters less than the outcome.

From Isolated Techniques to an End-to-End Attack Process

Traditional security analysis often examines attacker behavior as a collection of individual techniques:

  • SQL injection
  • Web-shell deployment
  • Credential discovery
  • Privilege escalation
  • Remote service access
  • Lateral movement
  • Data collection
  • Log or artifact deletion

Viewed individually, none of these techniques are new. What stood out in these incidents was how quickly they were connected into coherent attack sequences.  The environments and access paths were different. The attacker behavior was not.  Like any attacker, reconnaissance was performed to identify potential weaknesses in systems.  Then, the attacker exploits those weaknesses and moves on to further their objectives.

Incident Pattern One: Database Access Becomes Enterprise Access

In one case, the threat actor turned access to SQL infrastructure into a broader enterprise intrusion.

The observed activity included:

1. Web Application enumeration

The threat actor was observed probing multiple web applications in parallel and attempted to enumerate directories with varying degrees of success.  This is typical of blind application scanning when the adversary does not know sub-directories or the layout of the application.

2. SQL and web application probing

Internet-facing systems received repeated SQL injection techniques. This ultimately resulted in the successful enabling of xp_cmdshell.  Also notable was that the web application enumeration observed leading up to the successful xp_cmdshell activity stopped.

3. Command execution through database services

Subsequent telemetry showed SQL Server processes launching command shells and PowerShell consistent with the use of xp_cmdshell. The attacker used common discovery commands, tested remote command execution, enumerated linked servers, and assessed whether SQL functionality could be used to reach additional hosts.

4. Privilege-escalation attempts

The attacker staged or executed tooling consistent with token impersonation and service-account privilege escalation. In some instances, output files were used to check whether commands had reached a higher-privileged security context. Several privilege-escalation events were observed from the available telemetry.

5. Credential discovery and collection

Activity included searches through configuration and script files, attempts to save sensitive Windows registry hives, detection of LSASS-related credential access, and inspection of stored credentials and application secrets. Some credential-harvesting activity was blocked by endpoint controls.

6. Lateral movement at scale

The attacker queried administrative shares, tested remote SQL access, used WMI and scheduled tasks, and created remote tasks configured to execute under privileged accounts. Multiple servers were tested in quick succession.

Once xp_cmdshell was enabled, it would execute under the database server account.  In this instance, like many others, this was a service account on the server with high privileges.  This sequence demonstrates how a service account or database execution context can become a launch point for enterprise-wide discovery. This is not new. 

This is typical of activity observed with human operators, but the speed of pivoting and follow-on telemetry pointed to automated actions.  A database server may appear to be a specialized application asset, but its network reach, service credentials, linked servers, administrative tools, and access to other systems can make it a powerful pivot point for attackers.  From the start of web application enumeration to gaining xp_cmdshell was 1 hour 45 minutes.  The time on target until hosts were isolated was 30 minutes.

Incident Pattern Two: A File Upload Becomes a Cloud and Data Access Path

The second investigation followed a different route but produced a similarly broad attack sequence.

Application activity indicated abuse of account-management or password-reset functionality, followed by access to customer-related application data and use of an upload endpoint that accepted server-executable files. The attacker then deployed multiple web shells across several web servers.

Once established, the attacker moved quickly:

1. Web Application enumeration

Like the earlier incident, the threat actor was observed probing multiple web applications in parallel.  However, of note, was that once the webshell was uploaded on the first, the scanning of other applications persisted.  Ultimately 2 web applications were exploited, however this was the same code-base as it was a dev and prod version of the same site.

2. Web-shell execution

IIS worker processes launched command shells under application-pool identities. The attacker issued identity checks, listed websites and application pools, enumerated users and administrators, and explored accessible directories.

3. Configuration and secret harvesting

The attacker read multiple web.config files and searched for private keys, certificates, deployment profiles, environment files, unattended-installation files, and stored Windows credentials. Not only did this focus on web.config files in the application directories, but it also searched across multiple drives which found Service Principal Names (SPN’s) for applications no longer in use.  Those collected SPN’s were later seen attempting logons from suspicious IP addresses.

4. Cloud credential discovery

Commands queried the instance metadata service and attempted to recover temporary cloud credentials. The attacker also compiled and ran a dedicated metadata-access utility on multiple compromised systems.

5. Production database access

Credentials recovered or available in the environment were used to connect to production and staging SQL systems. The attacker enumerated databases and tables and submitted queries. Our investigation noted queries were run, but to obtain meta data about the database and were not observed doing bulk data extraction.  

6. Internal service access

The attacker found credentials for an internal file-transfer service, enumerated directories, tested write access, requested several files, and probed the host for additional reachable services.   This was associated with internal FTP services and leveraged obtained credentials found stored in plain text files across the systems.  Attempts were made to access RDP on multiple remote systems but were unsuccessful.

7. Privilege escalation and cleanup

The attacker retrieved privilege-escalation tooling, staged custom loaders, compiled utilities using software already present in the environment, and later issued commands to delete temporary directories and shell copies.

In this incident, it took the threat actor just over 3 hours to identify and exploit a file upload vulnerability.  Once webshells were successfully uploaded and executed, the threat actor remained on target for 1 hour 45 minutes before the affected systems were isolated.  

The investigation confirmed web-shell execution, credential and configuration discovery, database-access activity, internal service access, and cleanup attempts.  What was also discovered was that a critical business application was running on the same systems as a much older and less critical site.  While not directly targeted, the critical application became part of the blast radius when the older and vulnerable site was exploited.  

Why This Resembles AI-Assisted Intrusion Activity

In both incidents cited above, threat actors achieved initial access in under 3 hours. A recent Gambit Security report [1] documented a campaign in which open-source AI harnesses performed vulnerability discovery and exploitation against hundreds of online retailers. Between September 10 and September 15, 2026, the researchers identified 105 attack projects and at least 27 organizations compromised to varying degrees. The reported campaign used three components: Strix for vulnerability research, Cairn for autonomous exploitation, and Hermes for orchestration and operator guidance.

On October 23, PHP released an informational advisory disclosing another remote code execution vulnerability (CVE-2026-115560). The advisory states that the issue requires “an unusual combination of configuration and application code” and that mitigations published for PHP2Shell vulnerability CVE-2026-109619 also address this threat. Sophos will continue to monitor the vulnerability and will release updated information and additional countermeasures as appropriate. 

SophosLabs has also released additional PHP2Shell countermeasures, specifically Sophos Firewall and Endpoint IPS signatures 213184, 213185, 213187, 213188, and 213189.

October 22 21:21 UTC: Correction and new insights, countermeasures, and indicators

The previous update (October 22 16:18 UTC) reported that Sophos observed successful exploitation of PHP2Shell in customer environments. Upon further analysis, we are correcting that assessment as Sophos customer telemetry shows scanning and a small number of failed exploitation attempts. As of this update, there is no evidence of a successful compromise due to these vulnerabilities.

The payload, a likely Mirai botnet variant known as Potassium, was not delivered since the exploitation attempt was unsuccessful due to being blocked by Sophos countermeasures. However, analysis of the sample revealed that is an updated and significantly expanded version of the Mirai-derived botnet variant identified in early 2026. The sample displays downloader and network disruption functionality. It resolves a hard-coded, encrypted C2 address; establishes a TCP connection to 134[.]199[.]154[.]64; and sends an HTTP request. It checks for an HTTP 200 response status and verifies that the resulting payload begins with the ELF magic bytes 7F 45 4C 46, indicating that it expects to retrieve a Linux ELF follow-on payload. A resolver function supports IPv4 addresses and hostname resolution, with additional fallback resolution logic that includes hard-coded public DNS servers such as 8.8.8.8, 1.1.1.1, and 1.0.0.1. As with Mirai malware historically, this sample can execute DDoS attacks.

Sophos analysis of the vulnerabilities suggests that developing a successful exploit is not straightforward. The Sophos Adversary Group has been attempting to produce a successful exploit, which is proving challenging even with AI support. The lack of successful exploits in the wild suggests threat actors are also struggling. Security researchers have claimed they have developed successful exploits, but it is possible these only work in lab scenarios rather than real-world environments. Successful exploitation may also require certain dependencies or configurations. Despite the low level of activity, the vulnerabilities remain serious. Given time, threat actors may develop successful exploits. Urgent patching remains the primary recommendation.

Overview

On October 20, 2026, PHP announced an upcoming security release to address two critical (CVSS score of 9.2) vulnerabilities. Third-party sources identified the vulnerabilities as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. According to reports, the issues impact multiple PHP versions and allow for remote code execution. 

On October 21, PHP released updated versions to address these issues and stated that “all PHP installations serving web requests” are at risk. A user on the X platform claims to have created a working proof-of-concept exploit. As of this publication, active exploitation has not been reported in the wild.

Recommended actions

Counter Threat Unit™ researchers recommend that customers identify potentially vulnerable systems and upgrade as appropriate. In the interim, organizations should consider taking internet-facing PHP-powered systems offline if feasible or putting them behind network-layer authentication (e.g., ZTNA). Additionally, network defenders should evaluate the potential for exploitation in their environment and monitor for suspicious activity. The PHP advisory lists mitigations for organizations who cannot immediately upgrade but notes that updating is the only complete solution.

item.title: Is “SIEM-less” really what it sounds like?
item.description:
A SIEM is a multipurpose tool. It brings together cyber and physical security use cases; drives threat detection, investigation, and response (TDIR); serves as a system of record for governance, regulatory, and compliance needs; and supports observability use cases tied to resilience and service degradation. The list goes on.

In short, a SIEM is what an organization wants it to be. Therein lies both its strengths and its weaknesses.

The SIEM paradox

A SIEM can be a powerful “single pane of glass.” But that strength comes with two persistent challenges: operational complexity and data-ingestion costs.

Does more data mean better outcomes?

SIEMs store vast amounts of data. As the attack surface expands, organizations keep adding sources. Yet not all data serve the same purpose:

  • Detection and prevention require one set of data.
  • Investigations need contextual data to explain what happened.
  • Audit and compliance depend on evidence retained for reporting and review.

Because teams cannot always predict what they will need in the future, the default is often to ingest everything “just in case.” That is where the problems begin to compound.

Complexity comes first

The first symptoms are operational. Teams must determine which data is useful, why it matters, and how it should be applied in a particular context. Then they must be able to find it, search it, report on it, and turn it into something actionable when the moment comes.

Then comes the bill

Once the operational burden is established, the financial impact follows, often in the form of escalating ingestion costs.

How the SIEM became the center of the SOC

Over time, the SIEM also subsumed technologies that had once stood alone such as threat intelligence platforms, user and entity behavior analytics (UEBA), and security orchestration, automation, and response (SOAR). Each addition promised better context, stronger detection, or a tighter response loop.

Very quickly, the SOC was built around the SIEM, and the SIEM became fossilized in SOC processes and vendors took advantage of the “lock in”. Enter the era of SIEM deconstruction, and with it, the promised benefits of going “SIEM-less.”

Deconstructing the SIEM

Ingestion-based pricing crushing you with costs? Not to worry. Add a smart ingestion pipeline that filters out what you do not need before you store it. While you are at it, run detections in the pipeline. Et voilà, you have reduced storage costs and gained detections along the way.

Need to search the data in place? Add another component that can search across sources by translating queries for each one. Need to triage and investigate all those “detections” to determine what is worth chasing? Add an agentic SOC that promises to automate it all away.

Pretty soon, the collection starts to sound a lot like security information and event management, a SIEM. The difference is that the costs are now spread across individual components. It starts to look like unbundled pricing, where savings in one place create compute costs, or compromises, somewhere else.

The real cost driver: Compute

It is important not to confuse data-ingestion costs with storage costs. Processing data for upstream use cases requires compute; deciding how much data to retain, and for how long, requires storage. Even at today’s storage prices, compute costs dwarf storage costs.

Compute is the real cost driver. It is consumed when data is filtered, indexed for faster retrieval, queried, or used to generate reports. More compute is required when data must be rehydrated, moved from cold storage back into hot storage for analysis. Any or all of these costs can ultimately be passed on to the buyer.

A deconstructed architecture does not eliminate the underlying tasks or the ‘jobs to be done’. They still exist; they are simply carried out differently than they would be in a traditional SIEM.

Is SIEM-less a bad idea?

Actually, no. It can be the right call for an organization with the expertise and resources to build and maintain such a system. These new approaches are reshaping the economics and forcing traditional vendors to rethink their go-to-market strategies.

But a SIEM is ultimately a set of capabilities assembled into an architecture. Over time, every vendor offering one piece of the SIEM-less story will add adjacent capabilities until the resulting offering starts to look like, you guessed it, a SIEM.

Organizations that need a SIEM, therefore, face a practical choice: take the DIY route or invest in a fully integrated system with the right economics. At the end of the day, that choice matters.

So, where does XDR fit into all of this? More on that in my next blog.
